tip: 'Kata' + person = 'X says': 'kata siapa?' = says who?; 'kata ibu, boleh' = mom says it's allowed.
'Bilang ke' + person = tell that person: 'dia bilang ke saya' = he told me.
'Bahwa' ('that') is written-style; speakers usually drop it: 'dia bilang (bahwa) dia setuju'.
'Belum tentu' is literally 'not yet certain' – the Indonesian 'not necessarily': 'kabar itu belum tentu benar' = that news isn't necessarily true.
'Bilang' + person + 'supaya' + verb = tell them to do it: 'bilang ke sopir supaya menunggu' = tell the driver to wait.
After 'bilang', spoken Indonesian often uses 'kalau' for 'that': 'dia bilang kalau macet'.
'Siapa-siapa' after a negative = anyone: 'jangan bilang ke siapa-siapa'.
'Katanya' = 'they say / (s)he said' – a one-word rumor marker: 'katanya besok libur'.
'Dulu' has two jobs: after 'sejak' it means long ago ('sejak dulu' = since way back), but after a verb it means 'first' ('makan dulu' = eat first). Position decides.
'Menurut saya' is literally 'according to me' – 'menurut' means 'following'. Indonesian frames opinions like citing a source, even when the source is you.
'Menurut' also cites sources: 'menurut peta' = according to the map.
'Saya rasa' = I feel / I'd say – a soft opinion: 'saya rasa itu cukup'.
'Saya pikir' also = 'I thought (wrongly)': 'saya pikir kamu sudah pulang'.
'Pernah' packs 'have ever, at least once' into one word: 'kita pernah bertemu' = we have met before. The negative is 'belum pernah' = never (so far).
'Saya pikir' X, 'ternyata' Y is the stock reversal frame: 'saya pikir ini mudah, ternyata sulit' = I thought it was easy – turns out it's hard ('ternyata' = it turns out).
Ask opinions with 'menurut kamu...?' – starting with 'kamu pikir...?' often sounds like an accusation.
'Apakah' opens a yes/no question: 'apakah kamu setuju?' = do you agree?
'Kurang' softens a no: 'kurang setuju' = don't quite agree, 'kurang suka' = don't really like.
'Tanya' + question word reports a question: 'dia tanya kapan kita datang'.
'Apakah' mid-sentence = 'whether': 'dia tanya apakah saya lapar'.
'Jadi' before a verb = 'actually end up': 'jadi berangkat?' = still going?
The '-kan' ending changes what 'tanya' points at: plain 'tanya' takes the person you ask, 'menanyakan' takes the topic – 'menanyakan harga' = ask about the price.
'Bagaimana cara' + verb = how to: 'bagaimana cara memesan tiket?'
'Terus' after a verb means 'keep on': 'tanya terus' = keeps asking. The order flips English – 'keep' comes after the verb, not before it.
'Rasanya' = 'it feels / the taste of it': 'bagaimana rasanya?' = how is it?
'Sempat' = had a spare moment and used it: 'sempat tanya kabar' = found a moment to ask after your family. No single English word covers it.
Big prices stack left to right: 'dua ratus lima puluh ribu' = 250,000.
'Se-' here means one: 'semalam' = one night, so 'empat ratus ribu semalam' = 400,000 per night. Same trick: 'sehari' = per day, 'seminggu' = per week.
'Belas' = -teen, 'puluh' = tens: 'lima belas' = 15, 'lima puluh' = 50.
'Biaya kirim' = shipping cost, but shops and apps nearly always shorten it to 'ongkir' (from 'ongkos kirim'). 'Gratis ongkir' = free shipping – you'll see it everywhere.
